pharm: A five-carbon sugar alcohol used as a low-calorie sweetener that is not fermented to acid by oral bacteria, inhibits Streptococcus mutans, and is used in dental products, nasal/throat preparations, and as a humectant.

summary: Xylitol is a naturally occurring five-carbon sugar alcohol (polyol) used as a low-calorie sweetener and as a non-cariogenic agent in chewing gum, lozenges, toothpaste, and some nasal and throat products. Unlike sucrose it is not fermented to acid by cariogenic oral bacteria and it inhibits the growth and adherence of Streptococcus mutans, reducing dental caries and plaque. It has a low glycemic index and provides about 2.4 kcal/g. Excessive intake causes an osmotic laxative effect (bloating, diarrhea). It is highly toxic to dogs (causing hypoglycemia and liver failure) though not to humans. This is a supplement/non-drug entry based on reference information.
indications: Reduction of dental caries and plaque (non-cariogenic sweetener in gum, lozenges, toothpaste)
Low-calorie/low-glycemic sweetener for general use and in diabetes-friendly products
Adjunct in some nasal sprays and throat/oral-care preparations as a humectant/antimicrobial
Investigational/adjunct reduction of acute otitis media in children (via xylitol gum/syrup)

Introduce gradually to assess gastrointestinal tolerance

moa: Xylitol is a sugar alcohol that the major cariogenic oral bacteria, especially Streptococcus mutans, cannot ferment into acids; this deprives them of an energy source and reduces acid attack on tooth enamel. Xylitol is taken up by S. mutans but cannot be metabolized, accumulating as xylitol-5-phosphate in a futile cycle that inhibits bacterial growth and reduces plaque adhesion. It also stimulates salivary flow when chewed, aiding remineralization and clearance. As a sweetener it is absorbed slowly and metabolized largely independently of insulin, giving it a low glycemic effect; unabsorbed xylitol in the gut exerts an osmotic effect that accounts for its laxative action at higher intakes.

absolute: Hereditary fructose intolerance is not a concern, but rare polyol intolerance
Administration to dogs (veterinary contraindication - highly toxic)
relative: Irritable bowel syndrome or other conditions sensitive to fermentable polyols (FODMAP sensitivity)
Very young children prone to choking on gum/lozenges

preg: Xylitol in normal dietary and dental-care amounts is considered safe in pregnancy; excessive intake may simply cause gastrointestinal upset.
lact: Xylitol in normal dietary and dental amounts is considered safe during breastfeeding.
renal: No specific restriction in usual dietary or dental amounts; very large intravenous loads (a historical, now-abandoned use) caused metabolic problems, but oral dietary use is not a renal concern.
hepatic: No specific restriction in usual amounts for humans. (Note: in dogs, xylitol causes acute hepatic failure - this does not apply to people.)

major: No clinically significant human drug interactions
moderate: Other osmotically active polyols (sorbitol, mannitol) - additive laxative/GI effect
minor: May modestly slow oral bacterial metabolism (a desired dental effect, not a drug interaction)
interactions.food: Can be consumed with or between foods; use after meals enhances the dental benefit.
interactions.diagnostics: Does not meaningfully interfere with standard laboratory tests; minimal effect on blood glucose at usual intakes.

serious: None expected in humans at usual intakes
emergency: None in humans (note: ingestion by dogs is a veterinary emergency causing hypoglycemia and liver failure)

monitoring: Gastrointestinal tolerance, particularly with higher intakes
Dental health outcomes when used for caries reduction
counsel: Xylitol helps protect teeth and is a low-calorie sweetener, but too much can cause bloating or diarrhea - increase your intake gradually
For dental benefit, chew xylitol gum or use lozenges after meals and snacks
Keep xylitol gum, sweets, and products away from dogs - it is very poisonous to them even in small amounts
If you have a sensitive gut or IBS, you may tolerate only small amounts
It does not significantly raise blood sugar at normal amounts but still counts toward total intake
pk: Sweetening/dental effect is immediate on use
Slowly and incompletely absorbed from the gut
Rapidly metabolized once absorbed (largely via the liver, insulin-independent)
Dental antibacterial effect persists with regular repeated exposure
Store in a cool, dry place; keep containers closed and away from pets
pearls: Supplement/non-drug entry: a polyol sweetener that is non-cariogenic and inhibits Streptococcus mutans
Dental benefit depends on frequency of exposure (e.g., gum after meals), not just total dose
Low glycemic index (~2.4 kcal/g) - useful as a sugar substitute, but excess causes osmotic diarrhea
Highly toxic to dogs (hypoglycemia and acute liver failure) - a key counseling point for pet-owning patients
Generally recognized as safe for humans; no significant human drug interactions
missed: Not applicable - xylitol is a sweetener/dietary agent rather than a scheduled medicine. Resume normal use as desired; for dental benefit, simply continue regular use after meals and snacks.
overdose: In humans, excessive xylitol intake mainly causes gastrointestinal effects (bloating, abdominal cramps, and osmotic diarrhea), which are self-limiting; reduce intake and maintain hydration. (In dogs, ingestion causes life-threatening hypoglycemia and hepatic failure and is a veterinary emergency.)
